title: Browser and Events
summary: Find and change page elements safely, steer events through capture and bubble, use the browser's storage, history, fetch and timers, and investigate it all with Dev Tools.

lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, evaluate and manipulate the DOM.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body:
A web page starts as HTML: text full of **tags** like `

` and `

cards.title: Nodes and the document
cards.body: Every box in the tree is a **node**. Tags become element nodes, and the words between tags become text nodes. So every element is a node, but not every node is an element. At the very top sits `document`, the object for the whole page. It holds the search tools.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A big family tree on a wall. Each person is a box with a parent and kids. You can find someone by name tag, by group, or by a description. Where it stops: change a box in the DOM and the page on screen changes too. A wall chart never redraws itself.

cards.title: One, the first, or all
cards.code:
const form = document.getElementById('signup'); // one or null
const first = document.querySelector('.item');    // first match or null
const all = document.querySelectorAll('li.item'); // a list, maybe empty
const row = button.closest('tr');                 // nearest ancestor match
cards.body: Most finders take a **CSS selector**, the pattern CSS uses: `'.item'` means class `item`. `getElementById` and `querySelector` give one element, or `null` (JavaScript's "nothing here" value). `querySelectorAll` gives a `NodeList`, empty when nothing matches. `closest` climbs up through the parents, starting with the element itself.

cards.title: Live or snapshot?
cards.body: `querySelectorAll` returns a **static** `NodeList`: a snapshot taken once. Later changes to the page don't show up in it. `getElementsByClassName` (find by class name) and `children` (an element's child elements) return a **live** `HTMLCollection`. It updates by itself when matching elements come or go.

cards.title: Looping over the list
cards.body: A `NodeList` has `forEach()`, which runs a function once for each item. An `HTMLCollection` doesn't. Calling `forEach` on it throws a `TypeError`: the error for using a value the wrong way. Turn it into a real array with `Array.from()` first. Or loop with `for...of`, which works on both kinds of list.

cards.title: Wait for the page
cards.body: Code can only find elements the browser has already built. The `DOMContentLoaded` event (a signal from the browser) fires once the HTML is **parsed** (read into the tree) and **deferred** scripts have run. It doesn't wait for images or stylesheets. The `load` event on `window` waits for everything. Scripts with `defer` or `type="module"` also run after parsing.

`getElementById('#signup')` finds nothing: it takes a plain id, with no `#`. It returns `null`, so the next line throws a `TypeError` when it reads a property of `null`. Also, an empty `NodeList` is still an object, and every object counts as true in an `if`. So `if (list)` always passes. Check `list.length`, the number of items.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"All is a photo, getElements is a live camera."** `querySelectorAll` snaps once. `getElementsBy…` keeps filming. Single finders give one element or `null`.

lessons.title: Changing the DOM safely
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, evaluate and manipulate the DOM.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Once you have an element, you can change it. You can set its text, its CSS classes (style labels like `active`) and its **attributes** (settings inside a tag, like `id` or `href`). You can also build new elements. Some tools treat your string as **plain text**. Others read it as HTML and build real tags from it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A sign painter. `textContent` paints your words exactly as written. `innerHTML` reads your words as building plans and builds whatever they describe. Where it stops: a real painter would refuse a strange plan. `innerHTML` builds anything it is given.

cards.title: Text or HTML?
cards.body: `textContent` sets plain text, so `<b>` shows as the characters `<b>`. Reading it returns all text, even hidden text. `innerText` reads only the text a user can see. `innerHTML` parses the string as HTML and builds real tags. With user input, that is an **XSS** hole (cross-site scripting: someone else's script runs in your page).

cards.title: Build, then attach
cards.body: `createElement` makes a new `li` that is not on the page yet. The next three lines fill it in. Then `append` puts it at the end of `list`, with the text `' (new)'` right after it. `append` takes nodes or strings and returns `undefined` (no value). `appendChild` takes one node and returns it.

cards.title: Classes and data
items: `classList` holds the element's CSS classes: `li.classList.add('on')` adds one, and `remove` takes one off
`toggle` adds a class if it is missing and removes it if it is there. It returns `true` if the class is now on
`dataset` reads and writes `data-` attributes: `data-order-count` becomes `dataset.orderCount`. The value is always a **string**

cards.title: Attributes and more
items: `setAttribute()` sets any attribute and `getAttribute()` reads one: after `a.setAttribute('href', '/home')`, `a.getAttribute('href')` gives `'/home'`
`insertAdjacentHTML` parses an HTML string, like `innerHTML`. It puts the new tags at one of four spots: before, after, or inside at the start or end
`remove()` takes an element off the page: `li.remove()`

cards.body: **"Text for people, HTML only for code you wrote."** User data goes in `textContent`. `innerHTML` only gets strings you control.

An attribute that holds code to run when something fails to load, like a broken image. It runs even when added with innerHTML.

lessons.title: Event listeners and their options
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, utilize Events, event handlers, and propagation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **event** is the browser telling you something happened: a click, a key press, a form submit. A **listener** is a **function** (a set of steps you can run later) that the browser runs when that event happens. You attach it with `addEventListener`. The browser hands it an event object full of details.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A doorbell. You wire a bell (the listener) to a door (the element) for one kind of press (the event type). Press it, and your function runs. Where it stops: one door can have many bells for the same press. They all ring, in the order you wired them.

cards.title: Add and remove
cards.body: `addEventListener` takes the event type, like `'click'`, and the function. Adding the **same** function twice for the same type does nothing. To remove it with `removeEventListener`, pass that same function again. So after the last line, a click on `btn` runs nothing.

cards.title: Which element is this?
cards.body: `this` is a special word for the object the code runs for. In a regular `function` listener, `this` is the element the listener sits on: `event.currentTarget`. So a click before the removal makes `console.log()` print `true`. An **arrow function** (`() => {}`) is a short way to write a function. It keeps the `this` of the code around it.

cards.title: The options object
items: A third argument can hold settings: `btn.addEventListener('click', fn, { once: true })`
`once: true` removes the listener after its first run
`capture: true` runs it on the way down (next lesson)
`passive: true` promises not to cancel the event; a `preventDefault()` call is ignored, so scrolling stays smooth
`signal`: pass an `AbortController` signal; calling `abort()` removes the listener

cards.title: The older way
cards.body: `btn.onclick = fn` sets an **event handler property**. Each element has only one per event, so a second assignment replaces the first. `addEventListener` can stack many listeners. Use the property for quick demos and listeners for real apps.

Two arrow functions that look the same are two **different** functions. So `removeEventListener('click', () => save())` removes nothing. Keep a named reference. Also, the `capture` flag must match: a listener added with `capture: true` is only removed with `capture: true`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Same function, same flag, or it stays."** Removal needs the exact function and the same `capture` setting.

terms.say: A signal from the browser that something happened, like a click or a key press. Your code can listen for it.
A function you ask the browser to run when an event happens on an element. It gets an event object with the details.
The method that hooks a listener to an element for one event type, like click. You can hook up many listeners this way.
Unhooks a listener. You must pass the exact same function, and the same capture setting, that you used to add it.
An option that makes a listener run one time only. After its first run, the browser removes it for you.
An option that promises the listener will not cancel the event. The browser can then scroll smoothly without waiting for it.
Tells the browser not to do its normal job for this event, like following a link or sending a form.
An object with a signal and an abort() method. Give the signal to listeners or requests, then call abort() to stop them all at once.
An on-something property, like onclick. It holds one function at a time, so setting it again replaces the old one.
An option that runs the listener while the event travels down toward the clicked element, before it bubbles back up.
A set of steps with a name that you can run whenever you want. A listener is a function the browser runs for you.
A special word that points to the object the code is running for. In a regular-function listener, it is the element the listener sits on.
A short way to write a function, like () => save(). It has no this of its own, so it uses the this of the code around it.
Prints a value to the browser's Console so you can see it. console.log(1 + 1) prints 2.
The part of an AbortController you hand to a listener or a request. When abort() is called, everything holding that signal stops.
The AbortController method that pulls the plug. Listeners added with its signal are removed, and requests using it are canceled.

lessons.title: Propagation: capture, target, bubble
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, utilize Events, event handlers, and propagation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Click a button inside a card inside a page, and you clicked all three. So the event takes a trip. It travels down from `window`, the top object of the browser tab, to the button (**capture phase**). It reaches the button (**target phase**). Then it travels back up (**bubble phase**). Listeners along the path run as it passes.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A parcel delivered to a flat. It passes the city, the street and the building on the way in, and the empty box goes back out the same way. Where it stops: not every event comes back out. Some, like `focus` (a text box getting the cursor), don't bubble at all.

cards.title: Who runs first?
cards.body: Capture listeners on **ancestors** (parent, grandparent and up) run on the way down. Then the target's own listeners. Then **bubbling** listeners on the way back up. The `true` in the first line means "listen in the capture phase". With no options, `addEventListener` listens in the bubble phase. Here `log` stands for any function that records text.

cards.title: Three different brakes
items: `stopPropagation()`: stops the trip to other elements; other listeners on the **current** element still run
`stopImmediatePropagation()`: stops the trip **and** skips the rest of this element's listeners
`preventDefault()`: cancels the browser's **default action** (following a link, submitting a form); the trip goes on

cards.title: Reading the trip
cards.body: `event.eventPhase` is a number that says where the trip is: 1 capturing, 2 at the target, 3 bubbling. `event.bubbles` is `true` if this kind of event bubbles at all. `event.defaultPrevented` is `true` if a listener called `preventDefault()`. That only happens on a **cancelable** event; on other events it stays `false`.
"`stopPropagation()` stops the form from submitting." No. It only stops the event's trip, and the default action still happens. To stop the submit, call `preventDefault()`. To stop both, call both.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Down, hit, up."** Capture goes down, the target is hit, bubbling comes up. **Stop** stops the trip; **prevent** stops the browser.

terms.say: The first part of an event's trip. It travels down from the window toward the element that was clicked.
The moment the event reaches the element it happened on, like the button you clicked.
The last part of the trip. The event travels back up from the clicked element through its parents to the window.
The browser tab's top object. Events start their trip here and end it here.
Stops the event from traveling on to other elements. Listeners on the current element still run, and the browser's normal action still happens.
Stops the trip and also skips any other listeners on this same element that haven't run yet.
What the browser does by itself after an event, like opening a link or sending a form. preventDefault() cancels it.
A number on the event that tells where its trip is: 1 going down, 2 at the target, 3 coming back up.
Says whether an event's default action may be stopped. If it isn't cancelable, preventDefault() does nothing.
An event that fires when an element, like a text box, gets the keyboard cursor. It does not bubble up to the parents.
Every element above another in the page tree: its parent, its parent's parent, and so on up to the top.
Tells the browser not to do its normal job for this event, like following a link or sending a form. The event still travels on.
True or false: does this kind of event travel back up through the parents? A click does. A focus event does not.
True when a listener canceled the event's default action with preventDefault(). It stays false on events that can't be canceled.

lessons.title: Event delegation and custom events
lessons.objective: Given a business requirement, utilize Events, event handlers, and propagation.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Event delegation** means one listener on a parent handles events for all its children. It works because events bubble up. It saves memory, and it also covers children added later, like new rows in a list.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A school office. Instead of a phone on every desk, one office phone takes every call and asks who it is for. Where it stops: events that don't bubble never reach the office, so delegation can't catch them.

cards.title: One listener, many buttons
cards.body: `event.target` is what was actually clicked, maybe a tiny icon inside the button. `closest()` climbs up to the delete button. `!` means "not", so `if (!btn)` is true when no button was found, and `return` stops the listener there. `event.currentTarget` is `list`, where the listener sits. `removeRow` stands for your own code.

"`event.target` is the element with the listener." No, that is `currentTarget`. And `currentTarget` is only set while listeners run. Keep the event and read it later, say after an `await` (a pause until slow work is done), and `currentTarget` is `null`.

cards.title: Your own events
cards.body: A `CustomEvent` is an event you make yourself with `new`. It carries your data in `detail`. It does **not** bubble unless you set `bubbles: true`. Add `composed: true` so it can also cross out of a **shadow DOM** (a component's private inner tree). That matters in Lightning Web Components. `dispatchEvent()` fires it on `card`.

cards.title: Dispatch runs right away
cards.body: `dispatchEvent()` runs every matching listener **before** it returns. So the line after it runs after the listeners. It returns `false` if the event is cancelable and a listener called `preventDefault()`. Otherwise it returns `true`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Target got hit, currentTarget is listening."** Custom events stay put unless you say `bubbles: true`.

terms.say: Putting one listener on a parent instead of one on every child. Events bubble up to the parent, which checks which child was hit.
The element where the event really happened, like the exact icon you clicked. It can be deep inside the element that listens.
The element whose listener is running right now. Once the event is finished, it becomes null.
Climbs up from an element to the nearest one matching a selector, starting with itself. Great for finding the button around a clicked icon.
An event you invent and name yourself. It can carry your own data in its detail.
The box inside a CustomEvent where you put your own data, like a count or an id. Listeners read it as event.detail.
An option that lets an event travel up through the parents. Events you create stay on their element without it.
An option that lets an event leave a component's private shadow DOM. Add bubbles: true too, so the page outside can hear it.
A private, hidden tree inside a component. Its insides are kept apart from the rest of the page.
Fires an event on an element. All its listeners run right away, before the next line of your code.
Means "not". It flips true to false and false to true. !btn is true when btn is null, so nothing was found.
Ends a function right away. Any code after it in that function is skipped.
Pauses an async function until slow work, like a server call, is done. Then the function carries on. Other code can run during the pause.
Tells the browser not to do its normal job for this event, like following a link or sending a form.

lessons.title: Browser APIs: storage, history, fetch and timers
lessons.objective: Given a scenario and requirements, utilize browser specific APIs.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: The browser gives JavaScript extra tools that aren't part of the language itself. You can save data on the device, change the address bar, ask a server for data and run code later. These are **Web APIs**. Some, like the DOM and `history`, don't exist in Node.js, which runs JavaScript outside the browser.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A hotel. `localStorage` is a locker that keeps your things until you empty it. `sessionStorage` is the room safe: it empties when you check out (close the tab). Where it stops: both only take paper notes (strings). So turn an object into text with `JSON.stringify()` first, and back with `JSON.parse()`.

cards.title: Storage
cards.body: `localStorage` keeps data per **origin** (scheme, host and port), with no expiry. `sessionStorage` is per origin and per tab: it survives a reload but clears when the tab closes. Both store **strings** only. `setItem()` saves: `setItem('n', 5)` stores `'5'`, and an object becomes `'[object Object]'`. `getItem()` reads; a missing key gives `null`.

cards.title: History and location
cards.body: `history.pushState()` changes the address bar without loading a page. `replaceState()` swaps the current entry instead of adding one. Neither fires **`popstate`**; that fires on Back and Forward. `location.assign(url)` or setting `location.href` really loads a page. `navigator` describes the browser, like its language.

cards.title: Waiting for an answer
cards.body: `fetch()` asks a server for data. The answer takes time, so you get a **promise** right away: an object that will hold the result later. A promise **fulfills** when the result arrives, or **rejects** when something fails. `await` waits for the promise and hands you its value.

cards.title: Fetch: check ok
cards.body: `fetch()` rejects only when the request fails, like a network error or an abort. A 404 or 500 still fulfills. So check `res.ok`: it is `true` only for status 200-299. Here a 404 makes the code throw its own error, "HTTP 404". If all is well, `res.json()` reads the body as data. Cancel a request with an `AbortController` signal.

cards.title: Timers
items: `setTimeout` runs a function once, after a delay; `setInterval` repeats it. Both return an id for `clearTimeout` or `clearInterval`
The delay is a **minimum**: busy code, deep nesting and background tabs make it later
`requestAnimationFrame` runs code right before the next screen draw: best for animation
**Debounce**: wait until calls stop (search box). **Throttle**: at most once per period (scroll)

cards.body: "`fetch` throws on a 404." It doesn't. The promise fulfills with `ok` set to `false`. Only network errors and aborts reject. And `pushState` never fires `popstate` by itself.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Strings in storage, ok after fetch, ids for timers."**

terms.say: Extra tools the browser gives JavaScript, like storage, fetch and timers. They are not part of the JavaScript language itself.
A small key-value store in the browser for one website. Its strings stay after the browser closes, until someone removes them.
Like localStorage, but only for one tab. It survives a reload, and it is wiped when that tab closes.
A website's address family: scheme, host and port together. https://shop.com and http://shop.com are different origins with separate storage.
Adds a new entry to the tab's history and changes the address bar, without loading a new page.
An event that fires when the user moves through history, like pressing Back. Calling pushState doesn't fire it.
The browser's way to ask a server for data. It gives a promise for the response, even when the server answers with an error code.
Asks the browser to run your function just before it next paints the screen. It keeps animations smooth.
Waiting until calls stop for a moment, then running once. A search box waits until you pause typing.
Letting a function run at most once in each time slot, however often it is called. Handy for scroll events.
Turns an object into a string of JSON text. { a: 1 } becomes '{"a":1}', which storage can keep.
Turns JSON text back into a real object. '{"a":1}' becomes { a: 1 } again.
Saves a value under a key name in storage. The value is turned into a string first, so 5 is saved as '5'.
Reads the value saved under a key name. You always get a string back, or null if nothing was saved there.
An object that stands for an answer that is not ready yet. Later it fulfills with a value, or rejects with an error.
Waits for a promise to settle, then gives you its value. If the promise rejects, await throws the error instead.
True when the server answered with a success status, 200 to 299. False for answers like 404 or 500.
Runs a function once after a delay in milliseconds. setTimeout(fn, 1000) runs fn after at least 1 second. It returns an id.
Runs a function again and again, with a delay between runs. It keeps going until you stop it with clearInterval.
Stops a timer before it runs again. Give it the id the timer returned: clearTimeout for setTimeout, clearInterval for setInterval.

lessons.title: Browser Dev Tools: inspect, watch and measure
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, utilize the Browser Dev Tools to investigate code behavior.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Browser Dev Tools** are the toolbox built into Chrome and other browsers (press F12). They show the live DOM, run code, pause scripts, list network calls and measure speed. You use them to find out why the page does what it does.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A mechanic's garage. One bay lifts the car to look underneath (Elements). One plugs into the engine computer (Console). One films the engine running (Performance). Where it stops: most changes you make in Dev Tools are gone after a reload. They don't save to your code.

cards.title: Which panel?
items: **Elements**: live DOM and CSS, an Event Listeners pane, DOM change breakpoints
**Console**: run code, read logs and errors
**Sources**: **breakpoints** (pause points), stepping line by line, Scope (variables in reach), Call Stack (who called whom) and **Watch**
**Network**: each request's status, headers, response and timing
**Performance** and **Memory**: slow frames, CPU time, heap snapshots
**Application**: storage and cookies

cards.title: Console shortcuts
cards.code:
$0                    // element picked in Elements
$('.cart')            // like document.querySelector
$$('li')              // like querySelectorAll, as an array
getEventListeners($0) // listeners on that element
monitorEvents(window, 'resize') // log each resize
cards.body: These **Console Utilities** only work when typed into the Console. Your page's own scripts can't call them. `$()` works like `document.querySelector()`. `$$()` finds every match and gives a real array. `getEventListeners()` lists the listeners on an element.

cards.title: Smarter breakpoints
cards.body: You can pause on more than a line. An **event listener breakpoint** pauses when, say, any `click` listener runs. An XHR/fetch breakpoint pauses when a request URL contains some text (XHR is the older way to request data). A DOM change breakpoint pauses on code that edits a node. A **logpoint** logs a message without pausing.

cards.title: Network and memory
cards.body: Each Network row is one request: method, status, type, size and time. **Throttling** fakes a slow connection. "Disable cache" acts like a first-time visitor. "Preserve log" keeps rows across page loads. In Memory, a **heap snapshot** shows what JavaScript still holds, like detached DOM nodes (off the page but still kept) that leak.

"Fix it in Elements and you're done." Edits there live only in this tab, and a reload throws them away. Fix your source files. Also, `$0` and `monitorEvents` exist only in the Console. Called in page code, they throw a `ReferenceError`: the error for a name that doesn't exist.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Elements to look, Console to ask, Sources to pause, Network to fetch, Performance to time."**

terms.say: A toolbox built into the browser for looking inside a page. You can see the page tree, run code, pause scripts and watch requests.
The Dev Tools panel that shows the live page tree and its CSS. You can pick any element and see or change it.
The Dev Tools panel for your scripts. You set breakpoints there and step through code line by line.
A pane where you type expressions, like cart.total. While the code is paused, it shows their current values.
A Console shortcut for the element you last picked in the Elements panel.
Extra helper commands, like $0 and monitorEvents, that work only when typed into the Console, not in page code.
A Console command that prints every chosen event that happens on an element, like each key press.
A Sources setting that pauses the code whenever a chosen kind of event, like click, runs a listener.
A breakpoint that only prints a message to the Console. The code keeps running without pausing.
A picture of everything JavaScript holds in memory at one moment. It helps you find objects that should have been freed.
Markers that pause your code at a chosen spot. While it is paused, you can look at every value and step ahead one line at a time.

flashcards.front: What do `getElementById` and `querySelector` return when nothing matches?
flashcards.back: `null`. Both return one element or `null`. Reading a property of that `null` throws a `TypeError`.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `querySelectorAll` and `getElementsByClassName`?
flashcards.back: `querySelectorAll` returns a static `NodeList`: a snapshot that never changes. `getElementsByClassName` returns a live `HTMLCollection` that updates by itself.

flashcards.front: What does `element.closest(selector)` do?
flashcards.back: It climbs from the element up through its ancestors and returns the first match, starting with the element itself. No match gives `null`.

flashcards.front: When does `DOMContentLoaded` fire, compared with `load`?
flashcards.back: `DOMContentLoaded` fires when the HTML is read into the DOM and deferred scripts have run. `load` waits for images and stylesheets too.

flashcards.front: Why is `innerHTML` risky with user input?
flashcards.back: It parses the string as HTML. Tags like `` can run code: that is XSS. Use `textContent` for user text.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `textContent` and `innerText` when reading?
flashcards.back: `textContent` returns all text, hidden text included. `innerText` returns only the text a user can see.

flashcards.front: How do `append` and `appendChild` differ?
flashcards.back: `append` takes many nodes or strings and returns `undefined`. `appendChild` takes one node and returns it.

flashcards.front: How do you read a `data-user-id` attribute with `dataset`?
flashcards.back: Use `dataset.userId`. The `data-` part goes, and each dash plus letter becomes a capital letter (camelCase). The value is always a string.

flashcards.front: What happens if you add the same listener function twice?
flashcards.back: The second call is ignored, as long as the type and the `capture` flag match. Two separate arrow functions count as two listeners.

flashcards.front: What does `removeEventListener` need to work?
flashcards.back: The same event type, the exact same function, and the same `capture` flag used when it was added.

flashcards.front: What do the `once`, `passive` and `signal` options do?
flashcards.back: `once` removes the listener after one run. `passive` promises not to cancel, so `preventDefault()` is ignored. `signal` removes it when its `AbortController` calls `abort()`.

flashcards.front: What does `this` point to inside an event listener?
flashcards.back: In a regular function: the element the listener is on (`currentTarget`). An arrow function has no `this` of its own, so it keeps the outer one.

flashcards.front: What are the three phases of an event's trip?
flashcards.back: Capture (down from `window`), target (at the element), then bubble (back up). With no options, listeners run in the bubble phase.

flashcards.front: How do `stopPropagation()` and `stopImmediatePropagation()` differ?
flashcards.back: Both stop the trip to other elements. `stopImmediatePropagation()` also skips the remaining listeners on the same element.

flashcards.front: Does `stopPropagation()` stop a link or form submit?
flashcards.back: No. It only stops the trip. `preventDefault()` cancels the default action, and only for cancelable events.

flashcards.front: What is event delegation, and why use it?
flashcards.back: One listener on a parent handles events from its children through bubbling. It uses fewer listeners and covers children added later.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between `event.target` and `event.currentTarget`?
flashcards.back: `target` is where the event happened, like the clicked icon. `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running. It is `null` once the event is finished.

flashcards.front: How do you send data with a custom event, and does it bubble?
flashcards.back: Put it in `detail`: `new CustomEvent('pick', { detail: { id: 7 } })`. It doesn't bubble unless you also set `bubbles: true`.

flashcards.front: When do listeners run after `dispatchEvent()`?
flashcards.back: Right away, before `dispatchEvent()` returns. It returns `false` if a cancelable event was canceled with `preventDefault()`.

flashcards.front: How do `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` differ?
flashcards.back: `localStorage` lasts with no expiry. `sessionStorage` is per tab and clears when the tab closes. Both are per origin and store strings only.

flashcards.front: Does `fetch()` reject on a 404 or 500?
flashcards.back: No. The promise still fulfills (succeeds), with `ok` set to `false`. It rejects only on a network failure or an abort. So check `response.ok`.

flashcards.front: Does `history.pushState()` fire `popstate`?
flashcards.back: No. It changes the URL without loading a page. `popstate` fires when the user goes back or forward.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
flashcards.back: Debounce waits until calls stop, then runs once. Throttle runs at most once per time period while calls continue.

flashcards.front: Which Dev Tools panel do you use for what?
flashcards.back: Elements: DOM and CSS. Console: run code and logs. Sources: breakpoints. Network: requests. Performance and Memory: speed and leaks. Application: storage.

flashcards.front: What are `$0`, `getEventListeners()` and `monitorEvents()`?
flashcards.back: Console Utilities: the selected element, the listeners on an object, and a live log of its events. They work only in the Console.

flashcards.front: Which breakpoints can pause without a line number?
flashcards.back: Event listener breakpoints, XHR/fetch breakpoints, DOM change breakpoints and exception breakpoints. Conditional breakpoints and logpoints sit on a line.
